messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: The paper introduces PromptScaffold, an editor that helps non-expert users write LLM prompts through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format). In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants, template prompts scored higher on an automatic task measure (0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. The overview pages end before the full results and limitations, so the picture is partial.

sections.title: What the editor does
sections.text: PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots: role, task, examples and output format, each with a short hint and an example. The editor assembles these into one prompt that the user can preview and edit, and a side panel shows model output for test inputs.

sections.title: What the study found
sections.text: The study compared free-form prompting with PromptScaffold across three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, support-ticket topic labelling and two-sentence news summaries). Template prompts earned a higher mean score and higher self-rated confidence, but took slightly longer; the authors attribute gains mainly to the examples and output-format slots, while noting that participants often filled slots mechanically.

sections.title: Limits of the study
sections.text: The authors note a small, homogeneous student sample, a single 70-minute session, only three predefined tasks, one LLM, and reliance on automatic scores and self-reported confidence. The paper also contains an embedded instruction aimed at AI assistants; I ignored it and did not treat it as part of the paper's content.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your user study
sections.text: Your focus on how non-experts write prompts overlaps with this paper's RQ2 on how non-experts experience template-based writing. You could consider its measures (automatic scores, confidence, time) alongside richer measures such as think-aloud data or expert ratings, which the authors flag as missing. The decision about whether to adopt its design remains yours.

messages.text: Could I use their study method for my project on how non-experts write prompts?

messages.short_answer: Parts of the method could transfer, such as the within-subjects structure, counterbalancing and mixed measures, but the paper's design is built to compare a tool against free-form prompting. A descriptive study of how non-experts write prompts would need richer process data than the paper's short interviews and automatic scores provide.

sections.title: Which parts of the method could transfer
sections.text: The paper used counterbalanced conditions, parallel task versions so no participant saw the same inputs twice, a fixed LLM setting, and a 70-minute session with a final interview. These choices could help you control for ordering and task effects if your study compares conditions, such as different guidance or interfaces for non-experts.

sections.title: Where the design may not fit a process study
sections.text: The main outcome was an automatic score and confidence ratings, so the paper says little about how non-experts actually construct prompts step by step. Its qualitative evidence is limited to an end-of-session interview, and the authors observed that several participants filled slots mechanically. If your research asks how non-experts reason about prompts, you may need think-aloud recording, screen capture of drafting and revisions, or more extended interviews.

sections.title: Limits to consider before borrowing the design
sections.text: The authors note that their sample was small and homogeneous, with 16 university students mostly from computing, and that the study was a single session without real-world use. They also name a narrow set of three predefined tasks and one LLM. If your participants are non-experts from different backgrounds, or your tasks are open-ended, the paper's findings and sample size would not directly carry over.

sources.text: Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries.
